patient.chief_complaint: Persistent confusion and inappropriate speech after brief shaking episode, not returning to baseline over 30 minutes
patient.history_present_illness: A 42-year-old Asian female teacher was brought to the emergency department by her husband after a witnessed brief generalized convulsion at home. Her husband reports she had been complaining of a severe headache for three days and had been 'not herself' — forgetting words mid-sentence and seeming confused about the day of the week. She has no prior history of seizures or epilepsy. The shaking episode lasted approximately 2 minutes then stopped on its own, but she did not regain her normal level of consciousness. When EMS arrived 8 minutes after the seizure, she was awake but confused, answering questions with inappropriate words, and appeared agitated. In the ED she is minimally following commands, oriented only to her name. She has a history of SLE diagnosed 6 years ago, currently in clinical remission per her rheumatologist. She takes hydroxychloroquine and a low-dose prednisone taper she started 10 days ago for mild joint flares. She also takes levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily started 5 months ago after a first unprovoked seizure. Her blood pressure at home has been elevated per recent records. No fevers, no sick contacts, no recent travel.

results.finding: PRES occurs in 0.4-1.9% of SLE patients; hypertensive emergency is the most common precipitant; seizures occur in >70% of SLE-PRES cases
Full radiologic resolution in >90% of PRES with BP control; recurrence risk if BP poorly controlled long-term
PRES-associated NCSE responds to BP control + AED; EEG monitoring essential; DWI restriction in PRES predicts poor outcome
Absence of DWI restriction (vasogenic edema only) in PRES = good prognosis for full recovery
Elevated anti-dsDNA antibody and low complement levels (C3, C4) are serological markers associated with systemic lupus erythematosus disease activity.

output.summary: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) occurs in approximately 0.4-1.9% of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus; seizures are reported in over 70% of SLE-PRES cases. Hypertensive emergency is the most frequently identified precipitant. Radiologic resolution occurs in over 90% of PRES cases with effective blood pressure control. Absence of DWI restriction (vasogenic edema pattern) on MRI is associated with favorable outcome. Antiseizure medications have been used alongside blood pressure management in PRES-associated seizures. EEG monitoring is used for seizure detection in this population.
